title: The cry of joy
hookLine: bole so nihaal, sat sri akaal: whoever says it is blessed, true is the Timeless

cards: If you've ever been near a gurdwara on a big day, or at a Sikh parade, you've heard it. One voice calls out: bole so nihaal! And a whole crowd answers, louder than seems possible: sat sri akaal!

It can shake windows. It comes at the end of the Ardas, at weddings, at the start of a procession, sometimes from a single grandmother at the kitchen table when the news is good. It isn't a quiet prayer.
It's a cry of joy, and it has a name: the jaikara.

teach.b: Inside the word jaikara, some readers hear jai, victory or praise, the word in a cheer of triumph. It's a call and response.
The first half, bole so nihaal: whoever says it will be nihaal. Nihaal is a lovely word: blessed, fulfilled, full to the brim with joy.

teach.h: SAT SRI AKAAL: TRUE IS THE TIMELESS.
teach.b: The second half, sat sri akaal: true is the Timeless One. Sat is truth. Sri is a word of honor.
Akaal is the one beyond time, the name Sikhs use for God who has no beginning and no death.
Together: whoever says this is filled with joy, because the Timeless is true.
Sikh tradition links the jaikara with Guru Gobind Singh and the Khalsa, and in Sikh history it was raised before battle, a way of reminding fighters that the outcome belonged to the Timeless.
Today it's raised at every kind of moment.
And the second half has a life of its own: sat sri akaal is also an everyday greeting in Punjabi, hello and goodbye, with the truth of the Timeless folded inside. Now, the week just finished.
Day 631, vichhora, prayed for from across a border. Then maan: God as the strength of the weak. The petition, where the reason is named.
Bhul chuk. The last line, rising spirits, good for all. The couplet, Nanded.
And now the jaikara, the shout that closes it. A week that walked from grief, through humility and honesty, out into joy.

how: After the Ardas and at joyful or solemn moments, one person calls bole so nihaal and the congregation answers sat sri akaal; sat sri akaal is also an everyday Punjabi greeting.

o: a hymn sung softly at the start of kirtan
a joyful call and response: true is the Timeless
a quiet prayer said alone before sleeping

s: the jaikara is a whispered prayer
it's a call and response, often loud enough to shake windows.
sat sri akaal is also an everyday Punjabi greeting
hello and goodbye, with the truth of the Timeless inside.
the jaikara is only used before battle
it was raised before battle in history; today it marks every kind of moment.

games.q: one voice in the gurdwara calls out: bole so nihaal! what does the hall do?
games.why: the whole congregation answers together. whoever says it is filled with joy; true is the Timeless.

practice: Sit up and take a full breath, then, if you're somewhere you can, say it out loud: bole so nihaal, sat sri akaal; on a bus, say it inside, with the same full voice in your head.
Then sit with the echo, and notice what changed in your chest and shoulders. A jaikara isn't meant to be muttered; it's meant to lift, so stay with that lift, breathing.

wordCard.voice: Jaikara. The Sikh cry of joy: bole so nihaal, sat sri akaal. Whoever says it is filled with joy; true is the Timeless One.

carryVoice: Your line: sat sri akaal. True is the Timeless, in every hello and goodbye. Rest well.
